question: Compute and visualize the optimal segmentation model with 2 peaks for each ChIP-seq data set.

files.eval_guideline: Plot must show a 2-peak segmentation model for each ChIP-seq dataset with genomic position on the x-axis and coverage signal on the y-axis; colors, fonts, and panel arrangement may differ.
files.match_reasoning: The candidate has the identical filename and PNG image format as the reference. It directly corresponds to the requested visualization of the optimal two-peak segmentation model.
files.strategy_reasoning: The guideline requires semantic plot content—a 2-peak segmentation model for every dataset with correctly assigned genomic-position and coverage axes—while explicitly allowing visual styling and panel layout to vary. Semantic comparison is therefore appropriate for this PNG output.

comparison_details.explanation: Both images show constrained segmentation models with exactly two elevated peak segments for each of the same ChIP-seq experiments, H3K36me3 and H3K4me3. Their genomic locations and overall signal patterns agree closely: H3K36me3 has two broad peaks near 111650 and 111820, while H3K4me3 has two narrow, high peaks near 175460 and 175500. Both provide genomic position on the x-axis, coverage/count on the y-axis, observed signals, piecewise-constant model means, and peak boundaries. The candidate also explicitly highlights peak intervals with red bars. However, the plotted signal magnitudes differ materially: H3K4me3 reaches roughly 200 in the reference but nearly 370 in the candidate, with modeled peak means around 85–90 versus about 125; H3K36me3 also has somewhat different peak heights and one second-peak boundary. The reference additionally displays separate 'bases.counted: each' and 'bases.counted: end' rows, whereas the candidate shows only one coverage representation per experiment. Thus the requested two-peak scientific interpretation is preserved, but differences in signal representation, scales, and included data layers prevent full equivalence.
